newsitem.title: GERMANY: German municipality debts seen rising ahead of EMU.
newsitem.headline: German municipality debts seen rising ahead of EMU.

text.p: Germany's state districts on Tuesday said Bonn's austerity budget aimed to whip it into shape for European monetary union (EMU) is shifting an ever larger share of public debt onto local communities.
The total budget deficit for the country's 323 districts is expected to rise 100 million marks to 1.2 billion marks this year, said Rural District Conference (DLT) officials.
"The federal government disregards the fact that the indebtedness of local governments is growing ever larger," DLT President Axel Endlein told a news conference in Bonn.
Tax revenues for local communities were expected to fall one billion marks to around 72 billion marks this year, while expenditure would be cut 900 million marks to 73.15 billion.
Plans by Bonn to abolish taxes on commercial trading capital would also hit local governments hard.

This would be partially offset by earmarking a share of value-added tax for local communities, but Endlein urged the government to make these funds available this year rather than first in 1998 as currently planned.

As the federal and state governments sought to rein in public spending to meet the strict deficit limits in the Maastricht treaty, local communities were saddled with additional administrative expenses.

But Endlein said EU members would be judged by debts related to public investment budgets and not to the costs of public administration when the EU determines which of its members qualify for monetary union.

European governments hoping to participate in EMU must restrict budget deficits to no more than three percent of gross domestic product and total public debt to 60 percent this year to qualify for EMU in 1999.

As a result of deteriorating fincances at the local level, communities were being forced to drop plans for public investment, which was having an especially negative impact on infrastructure development in eastern Germany.
